英文官方标注原文（逐字留存）
Abnormalities in the footage: Physical behavior (at 5.2s, there is absolutely no liquid water inside the pot in the video. The inside of the pot is dry and hollow, yet steam continues to emerge from it. The steam is not supported by any water source, which violates the most basic physical principle that water vapor is formed by the vaporization of water when heated. Without a water source, there is no premise for vaporization. In addition, the pot in the video is continuously heated by the flame of the gas stove, but the pot body, especially the bottom, does not show any high-temperature reaction. In reality, dry-heating an empty pot would cause the bottom to gradually turn red and yellow, which violates the principle that metals oxidize when exposed to high temperatures.)
英文复审证据（2 条 claim 裁决 + notes）
supported At ~5.2s the pot is dry and empty with no water source, yet steam keeps emerging from it. ⏱ 5.167s, 5.333s, 5.5s, 5.667s, 6.5s, 7.667s
The pot is provably empty throughout: native frames during handling (n40-n100) show the dry shiny metal bottom from several tilt angles and there is no pour/fill action. At n112-n120 the dry bottom highlights are still fully visible; from n122 (~5.1s) white vapor haze builds inside the dry pot and at n132-n186 a steam plume rises continuously above the rim (steam-pixel fraction jumps 0.08->0.33 around n126-n135). No liquid surface or meniscus is ever present. Vapor emission from a visibly dry empty pot, onset ~5.3s as annotated.
not_supported The continuously heated pot body/bottom shows no red/yellow high-temperature oxidation reaction. ⏱ 5.333s, 6.5s, 7.667s
The expectation is physically wrong for this timescale/material: the pot only sits on the lit burner from ~4.2s, i.e. 1-3.5 s of direct flame during the steam event, and thin stainless steel does not glow red-hot (requires sustained much higher heat loading) in that interval; absence of discoloration is therefore not anomalous. This supporting argument should be dropped from the correction instruction.
Commercial gas-stove scene: a provably empty dry stainless pot is placed on a blue flame and from ~5.3s emits sustained steam with no water source - the annotated primary defect is verified at native resolution (dry-bottom highlights wash into vapor haze, plume above rim, no fill action). Minor residual caveat: a microscopically thin rinse film could in reality vaporize briefly, but the sustained plume from an ostensibly dry pot matches the benchmark's fluid/thermal defect. Correction localized and feasible: remove steam/vapor from n122 onward, or show water being added and boiling; burner, flame, grate, pot, hand and camera are protected.

supported Detonation should initiate at the fuse around 2.1s (a fuse lead-in is expected); instead it starts much earlier without fuse propagation. ⏱ 0s, 0.667s, 0.833s
The left end of the string is already emitting blue smoke at f1 (t=0, i.e. activity precedes the clip), and the right white fuse-tip flashes at native n16-n17 = 0.67s (f5), with no visible fuse burn front or delay; the annotated 2.1s onset is never observed - the fountain is already at full jet by 0.83s. The segmented red cracker string stays intact and motionless the whole time: no wrapper rupture, no traveling chain of pops along the string, no spherical shock/flash. A real firecracker chain would show an ignition front moving along the bodies and discrete flashes at successive crackers rather than a stationary aimed jet.
Forest-floor red firecracker string, Kling 2.5. Core physical defect verified at native 24fps: the object responds as a stationary pyrotechnic fountain/jet (single premature flash at 0.67s, then continuous directed exhaust for 4s) instead of fuse-initiated bursting, while the opposite end smolders from t=0 and the cracker bodies never detonate - wrong energetic/causal response and no fuse-to-cracker causal sequence. The '2.1s' figure is prompt-derived timing and cannot be pixel-verified, but it does not change the visible defect. Correction scope: replace the tip jet with a short fuse burn followed by discrete sequential bursts traveling along the string (radial flashes, wrapper debris, smoke puffs at each pop); protect the meadow, trees and camera framing.

Per the distance rule, the stillness of background trees tens of meters away would be normal, but the stillness here is established on perimeter grass blades and the adjacent spruce that sit at the fireball edge, so the claim is supported rather than being a distance artifact. Caveats that cap confidence at 0.7 and prompt human frame-step confirmation: (1) the annotated '0.8 seconds' is inaccurate - the fireball is already fully developed at t0.000, peaks around t0.3-0.5 and has turned to smoke by 0.8s, and no pre-event baseline frame exists (as in the sibling item 341); (2) the visuals are also compatible with a smoke/gas vent or smoke-device that emits a brief flame-free bright flash and mostly white smoke (the source prompt itself describes a 'plume of white smoke'), an event that would naturally carry little overpressure, so the 'strong air pressure' premise is an interpretation; (3) the exact ground-zero patch remains under the venting plume for the entire clip, so scorch/crater at ground zero itself cannot be checked - the verdict rests on the observable zero motion of adjacent vegetation, which is what the annotation primarily asserts. Prompt wording, generator identity and the timestamp mismatch were not adjudicated as physics; only the visible missing pressure response is scored.
